title: 1  Univariate Viz
text:
Use this file to generate a professional looking univariate visualization. The visualization will not perfect the first time but you are expected to improve on it throughout the semester especially after covering advanced topics such as effective viz.

Codeagencies <- read.csv ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/refs/heads/main/data/2025/2025-02-18/agencies.csv")

    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)

The Story Behind the Map






Answer



This map visualizes the average Airbnb listing prices across New York City’s boroughs in 2019. The data shows a clear spatial pattern, where the highest average prices are concentrated in specific boroughs. Notably, Manhattan stands out with the most expensive listings, reflected by the warmest colors (yellow/orange), indicating average prices around $250 per night. In contrast, boroughs like the Bronx and Staten Island display cooler tones (blue-green), suggesting lower average prices, closer to $100. The color gradient effectively highlights economic disparities within the city’s short-term rental market. It suggests that central, more tourist-attractive areas like Manhattan and parts of Brooklyn command premium prices, while more residential or less-touristy areas offer more affordable options. An important visual detail is the large grey area covering most of New York State. These counties are shown in grey because they either had no data available or were excluded from the analysis, as the focus here is specifically on New York City boroughs. This emphasizes Airbnb activity in New York really concentrates in urban centers.

Codelibrary(dplyr)
library(forcats) 

cleaned_fc <- fc %>%
  mutate(food_category = as.factor(food_category)) %>%
  mutate(food_category = fct_recode(food_category,
                                    "Lamb" = "Lamb & Goat",
                                    "Dairy" = "Milk - inc. cheese",
                                    "Wheat" = "Wheat and Wheat Products",

top5_countries <- cleaned_fc %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(total_consumption = sum(consumption, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_consumption)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Countries by Total Food Consumption",
       x = "Country", y = "Total Consumption (kg per capita)") +
